title: I Asked Claude to Design My Side Project. It Took Two Rejections and a Mascot.
partialText:
The full playbook: prompts, skills, a design linter, a mascot with six jobs, and the two audits where the AI found the bugs in its own work.

Every AI-designed product looks the same. You know the look before the page finishes loading: uppercase monospace labels tracked out like a terminal, a pulsing dot next to “Live”, rounded-2xl cards, a soft glow behind the hero, and an accent color that exists mainly to tell you a designer was not involved.

My site looked like that. I didn’t need a survey to know it. I could see it.

It’s a side project, not a business: free, no account needed, nothing to sell. That’s exactly why I wanted to see how far an AI could take the design when the only goal is that it’s good.

So I gave Claude the job of fixing it. Not a component, not a landing page: the whole brand. A new logo, a design language, a mascot, illustrations, every page of stackitfast.com and its sister site stackitfirst.com, and the shareable images the site generates on the fly.

Here is what shipped, in 27 commits between roughly 10pm one night and 9:30pm the next:

Commits                27
Files changed          230
Lines                  +13,265 / −7,901
Design-lint findings   418 → 0, enforced in CI
Contrast pairs         38 / 38 pass WCAG AA
Illustrations          25 (6 poses + 19 stickers)
Tests                  327 passing
Keyboard walkthroughs  16 / 16 passing
axe serious/critical   0 in 35 page × width scans
Merge to live          ~45 seconds

That’s the highlight reel. This article is about what it doesn’t show: the first logo round I called “really bad,” the design direction I rejected for being “ordinary,” the reference site that changed everything, the files that turned taste into rules the agent can’t ignore, and the two audits where Claude went back through its own work and found 34 invisible borders, a menu with zero height, and a way for one IP address to burn through my entire GitHub API quota.

If you want an AI to design something with personality, all of it matters.

Why AI design looks like AI design

A model doesn’t have taste. It has averages. Ask it for “a modern, clean, premium landing page” and you get the center of mass of every landing page it has seen, which in 2026 is a dark-mode SaaS template with a gradient and mono eyebrows.

That isn’t a bug in the model. It’s a bug in the prompt. “Modern, clean, premium” isn’t a design direction. It’s three ways of saying “do the default.”

Everything that worked in this project came from replacing adjectives with constraints:

  • References with a reason. Not “make it look like Linear” but “Linear’s mark works at 16px because it is one solid shape.”
  • Decisions written down as files. A rule in a skill survives the next session. A rule in a chat message does not.
  • Checks that fail. A design system the agent can violate without consequences is a suggestion.
  • Rejection, out loud. The most productive prompt in the whole project was two sentences long and not polite.

Round one: the logo, and the word “bad”

I started with the mark, because everything else would be built from it. The first prompt was ambitious and vague:

“I want to redesign my logo to strengthen our brand identity. Do a very detailed analysis, find the best skills for logo design, and design an eye-catching logo that reflects this project.”

Claude did the right homework. It found and installed a logo-design skill, studied the product (a directory of real production tech stacks, plus the rules files that let coding agents build them), and came back with three concepts on a proper presentation board: “Snap,” “Fold S” (marked as recommended), and “Prompt Stack.”

My reply, in full:

“All three logos you drew are really bad. I believe you can do better.”

This is the part most people skip, and it’s the part that matters. Claude didn’t argue and didn’t just iterate randomly. It asked why, with options, and I had to put the feeling into words:

  • crude, heavy, amateur
  • the wordmark is weak
  • it doesn’t say anything about the brand
  • the level I want: Linear, Vercel, Raycast

Those four lines did more than the original prompt. “Heavy” ruled out chunky geometric blobs. “Weak wordmark” moved attention to the type. The three references set the bar for craft: marks that are one confident shape, that hold up at favicon size, and that are shown in real context, not floating on a white artboard.

Round two produced the Stack File: one block carved into three layers that read as an S, with its top-right corner folded like a file, on a rounded apricot tile. A stack, a file, a letter: the product in one shape.

My reply that time: “I love the Stack File orange.”

Two things about the mark are worth stealing.

The geometry lives in code. The mark is defined once in `packages/ui/src/brand.ts` as a grid, a radius, a body path and a fold path. The favicon, the header logo, the app icons and the server-rendered OG images all draw from that one definition. When I noticed the favicon’s S looked bigger than the logo’s (“the favicon’s middle looks big but the logo is aligned”), the fix was to make the favicon stop being a separate drawing. One source, every size.

It was judged in context. The mark was checked the way it would actually be used: as a 16px favicon in a browser tab, in the site header, on a social card, as an app icon. A logo that only works at 512px on white isn’t a logo.

Round two: the design language, and the word “ordinary”

With a mark I loved, I asked for the system:

“Now let’s create new design skills from this logo and redesign the site to match it. I want a detailed analysis, a strong brand identity, a phase-by-phase plan, and a design fully in our new style.”

The first proposal was “sharp blocks”: the mark’s hard edges and folded corner carried into every card and button. It’s the bottom half of the first image in this article. It was tidy and coherent, and my reaction was immediate:

“You can do much better.”

When Claude asked what was wrong, the answer that came out was the most useful phrase of the project: ordinary, not premium. References: Stripe and Resend for polish, Raycast and Railway for personality.

Then I did the thing that actually unlocked it. I stopped describing and pointed at something: a playful product site, cut-noodle.com, with a character, sticker-style illustrations, a dark background with one loud call to action, the product working right in the hero, and cards people would actually share.

The important part was not “make it look like that site.” Claude asked what I liked about it, and I answered as specifically as I could:

  1. The character and illustrations.
  2. The dark ground with a vivid CTA.
  3. The product in the hero, not a screenshot of it.
  4. Shareable cards.

Four principles transfer. Pixels don’t. Before touching a single production page, Claude built the direction as a throwaway concept page in the component package’s preview app: an ink background, cream reading panels, apricot buttons with ink text, Manrope in sentence case, and a mascot made from the logo.

My reply: “Great, this is exactly the design I want. Now prepare a great plan for it.”

Lesson: you won’t describe your taste well in the abstract. You’ll describe it well while reacting to something. Get options on the table fast, say what’s wrong in plain words, and when you find a reference you love, say exactly what you love about it.

Turning taste into files: skills

A long chat thread full of design decisions is worth nothing the next morning. Context windows end, sessions restart, and the agent that redesigned your homepage at midnight doesn’t remember why the buttons have ink text.

So before redesigning any page, the plan’s first two phases built the foundation (tokens and components) and the skills: markdown files the agent loads on demand whenever a task touches UI.

.claude/skills/
├── stackitfast-design-system/
│   ├── SKILL.md        # language table + bans
│   ├── references/     # tokens, type, surfaces,
│   │                   # components, patterns, motion
│   └── scripts/
│       ├── design-lint.mjs     # fails CI on bans
│       └── contrast-check.mjs  # WCAG AA, real tokens
├── stackitfast-brand/          # mark, lockups, assets
├── stackitfast-illustrations/  # stickers, Stacky poses
├── design-refactor-page/       # migrate one page
└── logo-design/                # third-party, round one

The design system skill opens with the idea that ties everything together:

The interface is built from the logo. The mark is one block carved into three layers that read as an S, with its top-right corner folded like a file, on a rounded apricot tile. The UI keeps those parts and adds a character: Stacky, the mascot, is the same three layers with a face.

Then a table that maps every part of the mark to a UI rule:

Warm ink block
  The shell is ink; long reading sits on cream paper.
Apricot tile
  The ONE loud thing on a screen. Ink text, never white.
Three layers
  Compositions come in threes: ways in, stats, layers.
The fold
  The 45° folded corner marks files. Nothing else.
Rounded tile
  Panels 22px, controls 12px, chips 6px, icon tiles 22%.
Wordmark
  Manrope 800, sentence case, one emphasis word.
Character
  Stacky (6 poses) + stickers: 3px ink, hard shadow.

And a list of non-negotiables written as bans, because bans are easier for an agent to follow than vibes:

- No mono UPPERCASE eyebrows. A section label is a square
  marker + sentence case.
- No pulsing dots, no blur glow blobs, no gradients for
  decoration.
- No raw hex, no arbitrary text sizes, no
  shadow-lg/xl/2xl. Tokens only.
- No white text on apricot.
- No emoji in UI. Stacky and the stickers carry the
  personality.
- Every screen passes contrast-check.mjs and
  design-lint.mjs.

Read that list again and compare it with the “AI-designed” look from the top of this article. That’s not a coincidence. The fastest way to keep an agent away from the default is to name the default and ban it.

There’s also a surface decision tree, so the agent never has to guess:

1. Long reading (projects, rules, legal)?  → paper
2. Hero, listing header, tool, flow?       → ink
3. A file?                                 → the fold
4. Empty, loading, done or lost?           → Stacky

Rules the agent can’t ignore

Skills tell the agent what to do. Scripts check whether it did.

`design-lint.mjs` is under 200 lines of plain regex over every `.tsx` and `.astro` file. It knows 15 rules, including mono uppercase eyebrows, pulse animations, raw hex colors, arbitrary font sizes, banned shadows, legacy radii, pre-redesign surface classes, white/black overlays, 10px text, ALL-CAPS copy and emoji. The rare legitimate exception has to say why, right next to it:

// design-lint-allow rounded-full: avatars are round

When the redesign started, the linter reported 418 findings. It ran in warning mode while pages were migrated one phase at a time and the number came down. When it hit zero, CI switched to ` — strict`, so a new page in the old style now fails the build.

`contrast-check.mjs` reads the real token file and checks every foreground/background pair the UI actually uses: 38 of them, each with its WCAG ratio. When the audit later added a filled red “danger” button, it added the contrast pair for cream text on that red in the same change.

This is the difference between a design system and a design suggestion. With an agent writing hundreds of class strings an hour, the only rules that hold are the ones a script enforces.

The mascot: Stacky has six jobs

The character is the thing everyone notices first, and the thing that’s easiest to get wrong. A mascot slapped onto a template is decoration. We wanted one that does work.

Stacky is the logo’s three layers with a face: the top layer is the apricot file with its folded corner, and the middle layer gets eyes. It borrows the mark’s shapes (the layers, the fold, the apricot), so it reads as the brand even at footer size.

Every pose is tied to a product state in the skill, so “which Stacky goes here?” is never a creative decision the agent has to make.
pose="default"    section heads
pose="wink"       the hero, next to the survey
pose="wave"       sign-in prompts
pose="think"      loading, empty search results
pose="celebrate"  published, card made
pose="sleep"      404, nothing here yet

In code, a pose is just a prop, and the components that show states take an illustration slot, so the mapping lives where the state lives:

<EmptyState
  illustration={<Stacky pose="wave" />}
  title="Sign in to see your projects"
  action={<Button onClick={openLogin}>Sign in</Button>}
/>

The eyes blink on a slow loop, but only behind `motion-safe:`, so anyone who has asked their OS for reduced motion gets a still Stacky.

That mapping is the whole trick. “Add some personality” gets you a mascot on every surface, waving at nothing. “Stacky appears when the product has an emotional state, and the pose matches the state” gets you a 404 page that’s actually charming:

404 = sleep. Nobody had to decide that twice.

The stickers follow the same discipline. There’s a skill just for drawing them, with construction rules an agent can follow:

- Outline 3px ink, round joins; inner details 2–2.6px.
- Hard shadow: the same shape in ink, offset +4…+5px,
  drawn first.
- Wrap the drawing in a cream die-cut edge so it reads on
  ink.
- Badge: apricot circle, 3px ink ring, overlapping the
  frame by about a third.
- Grid: tool stickers 260×180, category stickers 120×120,
  Stacky 220×220.
- No gradients, no textures, no text inside illustrations.

Every illustration is a React SVG component, not a PNG, so it scales, themes and renders on the server for share cards. A script renders all 25 of them on ink and on paper into one contact sheet, so a new sticker gets checked by eye next to the existing ones before it ships.

Six tool stickers, thirteen category stickers. One hand, because the hand is written down.

Put the product in the hero

The biggest structural change wasn’t visual. The old homepage described the survey and linked to it. The new one is the survey: the first question and the team-size picker sit in the hero, and answering hands you off to the full survey with those answers already filled in.

This came straight from the reference (“product in the hero, not a screenshot of it”) and it changes how the page feels more than any color does.

Make the output shareable

The fourth principle was shareable cards, and it turned into the most fun feature of the project. Finish the survey, or paste any public GitHub repo, and you get a stack card in the brand language: a personality (“The Shipper,” “The Architect”), your stack by layer, Stacky celebrating in the corner.

The cards are SVG built from the same tokens and the same Stacky component, rendered to PNG with resvg-wasm inside a Cloudflare Worker. One image URL, three formats (`?format=post|story|og`), thumbnails (`?w=480`), cached at the edge. The share sheet on a phone hands over the image itself, so it lands in a story as a picture, not a link.

The rest of the site followed the same rules: ink headers, paper for anything you read, files with the fold, Stacky only where there’s a state.

The sister site got the same language with its own mark from the same geometry: an ink tile instead of an apricot one.

The plan that kept it shippable

The redesign ran as seven phases on one branch, in an order that kept every intermediate state working:

1. Foundation    tokens, Tailwind preset, components
2. Skills        design system, brand, illustrations
3. Homepage      the survey in the hero
4. Cards         share cards: survey and any repo
5. Pages         explore, project, editor, rules,
                 compare, insights, flows
6. Sister site   Stack It First
7. Brand output  OG images, badge; lint goes strict

Two process decisions worth copying:

  • Skills before pages. Phase two wrote the rules; phases three to seven only applied them. Every page refactor started with “load the design system skill,” so page twenty looks like page one.
  • One branch, not one per phase. I asked for it explicitly (“collect everything in one branch so we don’t get conflicts”). Seven parallel branches that all rewrite the same components are seven merge conflicts. One branch with one commit per phase is a reviewable story.

And one rule that never changed: pushing to main deploys, so merging was always my call. The agent built, tested and pushed the branch. It didn’t merge until I said “you can merge,” after both audits.

The part nobody posts: the AI audits its own work

Here is where most “I built X with AI” posts end: screenshots look great, ship it.

Instead, I asked for this:

“Now I want you to check everything top to bottom, find the problems, and make a plan to fix them.”

Claude launched three review agents in parallel, each with a different job (functional regressions, design consistency, and SEO/security/performance), then verified the serious findings itself before writing a plan. Verification matters: review agents produce confident false positives, so the critical findings were checked against the code or the compiled output before they got a line in the plan.

The headline finding was humbling:

34 borders on the site had never rendered. Not once.
The token was named onInk.lineStrong (camelCase). Tailwind
turns keys into class names verbatim, so it generated
border-on-ink-lineStrong. Every component used
border-on-ink-line-strong. No error, no warning: the class
just didn't exist, and the borders fell back to a default
gray. Unanswered segments in the survey progress bar were
invisible.

A human reviewer clicking around would probably never have spotted that, because “a slightly different gray border” doesn’t look broken. It was caught by comparing the class names in the source with the CSS the build actually generated. The fix was a small helper in the Tailwind preset that adds a kebab-case alias for every camelCase token key. The real fix was a test that compiles every token color class used anywhere in the source and fails if any of them produces no CSS. That bug can’t come back quietly.

The rest of round one:

HIGH  Mobile menu opened at 0px height: the header's
      backdrop-blur made it the containing block.
      Fix: portal the drawer to <body>.
HIGH  /r/<owner>/<repo> called GitHub with no limit
      and never remembered a 404.
      Fix: per-IP budget, 404 memory.
HIGH  Share links carry utm_ tags; robots.txt blocked
      /*?*utm_*, so link previews could fail.
      Fix: allow link-preview bots.
MED   "Welcome back" shown to first-time visitors
      coming from the homepage picker.
      Fix: the hand-over state.
MED   Every page queried the DB for a ticker the
      redesign had removed. Fix: delete it.
LOW   Legacy variants, dead CSS, stale docs.
      Fix: remove them; add lint rules.

Then I asked again, differently:

“Do another detailed check, like an expert QA engineer.”

Round two went after the things round one wasn’t looking for: keyboard and screen-reader paths, edge cases in the flows, and how the new features behave under abuse. It found real problems in code that had already been “fixed” once:

  • The rate limit was decorative. The “20 per hour” budget lived in each Worker isolate’s memory, while the shared limiter allowed 30 per minute. One IP could trigger about 5,400 GitHub API calls an hour against a 5,000/hour token. The fix is a per-IP and a site-wide budget on the shared limiter, verified in the Workers runtime: the sixth new repo in a minute gets a polite 503.
  • The cache could be busted for free. `?w=1`, `?w=2`, `?format=zzz`: each was a new cache entry and a new full-size image render. Now the cache key is built from the values the route actually renders.
  • The survey lost keyboard focus after every answer, and Enter on a focused “Back” button moved forward instead. The guard Claude added in round one only covered the review step. That’s a regression of its own fix, caught by the next pass.
  • Not-found pages were soft. Unknown rule slugs redirected to the listing, so search engines saw a 302 instead of a 404.

Then the verification. Not “I believe it works,” but scripts:

The keyboard scripts found one more bug while verifying the fixes. The new focus trap in the mobile menu relied on the browser’s Tab order, but the toggle button lives in the header and the menu is portaled to the end of the page, so Tab from the toggle jumped into the page behind the menu. The test failed, the fix went in, the test passed. That’s the loop you want.

I’m not going to pretend the agent is a substitute for a QA team. But an agent that reviews its own work in parallel passes, checks what the reviewers claim, writes the test that would have caught it, and then runs real browsers against the result found more in an evening than I would have in a week of clicking around.

The prompt playbook

These are the prompts that moved the project, cleaned up so you can reuse them. None of them are clever. All of them are specific.

1.Brand discovery: ask for options, not an answer.

I want to redesign the logo for [product]. Study what the
product does and who uses it first. Show three different
directions, each on a board with: the mark at 512, 64, 32
and 16px, the lockup with the wordmark, and the mark in
real context (browser tab, site header, social card).
Explain the idea behind each in one line.

2.Rejection: name what’s wrong, then the bar.

None of these work. They feel [heavy / generic / amateur].
The wordmark is [weak]. The level I want is [Linear,
Vercel, Raycast]: one confident shape that still reads at
16px. Try again with that bar.

3.Direction from a reference: principles, not pixels.

Look at [site]. What I like: [1. a character, 2. dark
background with one vivid CTA, 3. the product working in
the hero, 4. shareable output]. Don't copy it. Build our
own direction from our logo using those four principles,
as a throwaway concept page before touching real pages.

4.Write the taste down.

Turn the approved direction into skills under
.claude/skills:
- a design-system skill: the language as a table mapped
  from the logo, non-negotiables written as bans, a
  surface decision tree, references for tokens,
  typography, components, patterns, motion and voice
- a script that lints the codebase for every ban and can
  fail CI
- a contrast script that checks every color pair we use
  against WCAG AA
- an illustration skill with construction rules for the
  mascot and stickers
Load the design-system skill before any UI change from now
on.

5.Plan the rollout.

Plan the redesign in phases on a single branch: foundation
and skills first, then one area of the site per phase.
Each phase ends with typecheck, tests, lint and
screenshots at 1440 and 390px. Don't merge to main.

6.Audit, then audit differently.

Check everything top to bottom. Use separate reviewers for
functional regressions, design consistency, and
SEO/security/performance. Verify each finding against the
code before you believe it. Write a prioritized fix plan.
Now check it again like an expert QA engineer: keyboard
and screen-reader paths, edge cases in every flow, abuse
of anything public that spends a quota. Prove each fix
with a test or a scripted browser run.

When not to let the agent decide

  • Taste. The agent produced every pixel, but every direction was chosen by a human reacting to options. “Bad,” “ordinary” and “exactly this” were the three most important inputs in the project, and none of them could come from the model.
  • Production data. The one database migration (a cache table for repo cards) was written by the agent and applied by me, by hand, after reading it.
  • Main. Merging deploys. That stayed a human decision every time, including after two full audits.
  • Your own slop. A design system with a mascot can become its own cliché. If every page has a sticker, a wink and a tilted card, you’ve just built a different default. That’s why Stacky has six jobs and not twenty.

The checklist

□ Ban the default by name (eyebrows, glows, pulses,
  gradients, emoji)
□ Get three options, reject with words, raise the bar with
  named references
□ Judge marks in context: favicon, header, social card,
  never a white artboard
□ Put the brand geometry in code, one source for every
  size
□ Love a reference? Say exactly what you love about it;
  copy principles
□ Build a throwaway concept page before touching
  production
□ Write the language into skills: a table, bans, a
  decision tree
□ Enforce it: a design linter that fails CI, a contrast
  check from real tokens
□ Give the mascot jobs: one pose per product state, never
  decoration
□ Put the product in the hero; make the output shareable
□ One branch, phases in order, skills before pages
□ Audit with parallel reviewers, verify every finding,
  then audit as QA
□ Prove fixes with tests, axe and scripted keyboard runs
□ Humans own taste, production data and the merge button

The question

The redesign took 27 commits, two rejected directions and two audits. The AI wrote nearly all of the code and drew every illustration. I wrote a few dozen sentences of feedback, and the three that mattered most were “this is bad,” “this is ordinary” and “this is exactly it.”

So who designed it: the model that produced every pixel, or the person who kept saying no until it was right?

Everything in this article is live at stackitfast.com and stackitfirst.com. Take the survey to get your own stack card, or paste any public GitHub repo to see which personality it gets. The brand, design-system and illustration skills are installable from Stack It First with `npx skills add k61b/skills`.

title: Your AI Agents Don’t Know What Your Senior Engineers Know
partialText:
How I use instructions, automated checks, and shared context to make engineering knowledge available beyond a single conversation.

The different roles of instructions, automated checks, CI, and shared context in AI-native development

In my previous post, I wrote about the engineering system around the model: the specifications, context, tools, verification, and feedback loops that turn model capability into useful production software. I want to go a little deeper on one part of that system, because it accounts for a meaningful amount of the work involved in making agents effective.

An experienced engineer knows a lot about a codebase that the codebase does not explain. They know why a particular abstraction exists, which implementation is being retired, which seemingly reasonable approach caused problems before, and who is already working on something related. When they review a change, all of that context influences their judgment. They may spot a problem immediately without realizing how much background knowledge made it obvious.

An agent does not automatically have any of that. It has the instructions we provide, the code and documentation it reads, and the information it can retrieve through its tools. If something important exists only in my head, I cannot reasonably expect the agent to account for it.

That sounds obvious, but it changes how I think about corrections. When I tell an agent that it chose the wrong approach, part of the question is whether it had a reasonable way to know what the right approach was. And if I have made the same correction several times, I need to look at why the system keeps requiring me to supply it.

At Closedloop, this has led me to think about several layers of engineering knowledge and feedback: tribal knowledge, prose instructions, local deterministic checks, CI, and the knowledge graph available through Closedloop Intel. They overlap, but each contributes something different to the agent’s ability to do useful work.

The knowledge has to be available before it can help

Tribal knowledge is useful to the people who possess it. Until someone expresses it or makes it retrievable, it is effectively useless to an agent.

Our monorepo has a good example in the distinction between the design system and shared product UI. We have a generic component library in packages/design-system, and we have shared Closedloop components in packages/app. Both contain reusable UI. The distinction is that the design system is a separate, project-agnostic product, while the shared application package is allowed to understand our domain: sessions, branches, documents, projects, and the rest of the product.

If you have worked in the repository for a while, that boundary is familiar. If you are an agent asked to build a reusable component, “put it in the design system” is a plausible interpretation of the task. It may even look like good engineering. You are reusing code, avoiding duplication, and putting a component in the package whose name suggests that it owns components.

The missing information is why this particular component does not belong there.

This is where prose earns its place. Repository instructions can explain the boundary, the reason for it, and the correct home for the implementation. The agent can use that information while deciding how to approach the task, before it spends time building something we will have to move later.

I use prose at several different levels. Persistent repository instructions carry broadly applicable constraints. Skills describe procedures for particular types of work. Implementation plans capture the decisions and acceptance criteria for a change. Prompts supply the immediate request and any additional context that matters to it.

Those distinctions are useful because the information has different lifetimes. The ownership boundary between two packages may remain relevant for years. A decision about what to include in the first release of a feature belongs with that feature. A debugging procedure should be available when an agent is investigating a bug, without occupying every unrelated conversation.

The objective is to give the agent enough context to do the right thing on the first attempt. Clear prose can prevent a substantial amount of wasted work, especially when it explains a decision the agent could not confidently infer from the implementation alone.

It is also possible to overdo it. A repository instruction file can become an accumulation of every mistake an agent has ever made, complete with exceptions, repeated warnings, and rules that were written for circumstances that no longer exist. Maintaining those instructions is part of the work. More text does not necessarily produce more understanding.

The first attempt will still be wrong sometimes

Anthropic’s AI-native SDLC playbook uses a useful term for skills: advisory controls. They guide the agent toward applying a policy, but the instructions themselves do not enforce compliance. That describes the role of much of the prose around an agent. It can improve the decision without guaranteeing the result.

Even when the instructions are clear, agents will miss things. They will choose the wrong import, misunderstand a contract, or make a change that breaks an existing behavior. Some of these failures are predictable enough that we should not need a human to discover them repeatedly.

Hooks and deterministic checks give the agent feedback while it is working. Linting, typechecking, unit tests, and repository-specific gates can identify a problem before the change reaches review. Some hooks can intervene earlier still, blocking an action before it occurs — for example, an attempted edit to a protected generated file. Others run after an edit and give the agent information it can use to repair the implementation.

The design-system boundary has both forms of support. We explain it in prose, and we have a source gate that detects imports from prohibited domain packages. The instructions help the agent understand where the component belongs. The check catches a concrete violation if the implementation crosses that boundary anyway.

There is a limit to what that gate can establish. A component could contain Closedloop-specific assumptions without importing one of the prohibited packages. Recognizing that still requires judgment. But the import violation is a mechanical problem, and making a reviewer repeatedly catch it is a poor use of review attention.

I think this distinction matters when deciding what to automate. Some engineering expectations are difficult to express as reliable checks. Others are straightforward, but remain review comments because nobody has invested in making them executable. In an agent-heavy workflow, that investment becomes more valuable because the same class of mistake can appear across many independent sessions.

The quality of the diagnostic matters too. A failure that identifies the violated contract and explains where the code belongs gives the agent a reasonable path forward. A vague failure leaves it investigating the validation machinery before it can return to the actual task.

We also have to pay attention to what the agent changes while making a check pass. If it repairs the implementation by weakening the assertion, removing a difficult case, or changing the expected behavior, the green result may no longer tell us what we think it does. Tests sometimes need to change, but those changes deserve review against the requirement they were supposed to protect. Otherwise, the implementation and its verification can drift together.

The existence of a check does not establish its quality. A unit test can faithfully verify the wrong assumption. A source gate can cover only part of a rule. Typechecking cannot decide whether the feature solves the customer’s problem. These tools provide specific evidence, and I still need to understand what that evidence covers.

CI broadens the feedback

Local feedback needs to be fast enough that the agent can use it repeatedly. That creates practical limits on how much we run during every implementation cycle.

A formatter or a check scoped to the changed file can run frequently without interrupting the work very much. A full integration suite is a different proposition. Running it after every edit would consume time without necessarily producing useful new information. Waiting until the end to run every check creates the opposite problem: the agent may build several more changes on top of a mistake before discovering it.

Where we place validation determines both how quickly the agent can recover and how much work accumulates before recovery begins.

CI gives us another opportunity to perform more expensive checks, exercise broader dependencies, and evaluate the change in a controlled environment. In a monorepo, the scope difference is particularly important. A package can pass its own tests while breaking a consumer. Shared UI can behave correctly through one surface adapter and incorrectly through another. A focused test run may never exercise the boundary where the failure occurs.

Our repository has affected-package checks, broader verification commands, and separate validation lanes for different parts of the system. Shared product UI also needs consideration on both web and desktop, because sharing the component does not mean the routing, data access, or surrounding behavior is identical.

This gives the agent several opportunities to encounter useful feedback. It can catch an inexpensive mistake while editing, discover a behavioral regression in a focused test, and then encounter an integration failure in a broader run. Each opportunity should cover something meaningful at a cost appropriate to that point in the work.

As implementation gets faster, those costs become more visible. Verification runtime and coverage are part of the development system’s throughput, just as much as the time the agent spends writing code.

The agent also needs to understand the surrounding work

Instructions and executable checks address a lot of implementation mistakes, but they do not provide a complete view of what is happening around the task.

An agent can build a technically sound solution to work that someone else is already doing. It can make a reasonable local change without knowing that another project is replacing the underlying contract. It can read an implementation without finding the product decision that explains why it behaves that way.

This is where the knowledge graph available through Closedloop Intel fits into the workflow. It gives agents access to relationships between tickets, plans, code, branches, and pull requests. They can investigate scope overlap, follow the lineage of a work item, and look for dependencies or other work touching the same area.

That information helps the agent form a better picture of the problem before deciding what to do.

Suppose I ask an agent to add a capability to an existing feature. Code exploration can tell it what is implemented today and which abstractions are available. Ticket and dependency information can reveal that part of the request is already in progress, that another issue establishes a prerequisite, or that the work originated in a larger plan with constraints that are not obvious from the code.

Without that context, the agent may produce a coherent implementation that creates unnecessary reconciliation work for the team. Access to the surrounding work gives it a chance to recognize those relationships earlier.

The graph needs the same scrutiny as other information sources. Coverage and freshness matter. A recorded relationship is evidence to investigate, and claims about the current code still need to be checked against the relevant checkout. But this is a much more useful starting point than expecting every agent to reconstruct organizational context from whatever happens to be mentioned in its prompt.

It also reduces the amount of information I need to manually package for every task. I can give the agent a focused request and a way to discover relevant context, rather than trying to anticipate and paste everything it might need.

The environment needs evaluation too

There is another implication of putting more engineering knowledge into the agent’s environment: changes to that environment can change the quality of its work.

We are accustomed to testing the code an agent produces. We should also evaluate whether a revised instruction, a new skill, or a different hook actually improves the agent’s ability to produce it. A skill can be well written and still fail to load when needed. A new instruction can resolve one recurring mistake while creating confusion elsewhere. A model change can alter how consistently the same configuration is followed.

The Anthropic playbook recommends keeping representative tasks and their acceptance checks as an evaluation suite, then using that suite when the agent configuration changes. That seems like a useful extension of the same discipline. We would be checking whether the agent can still perform real work to the expected standard, rather than assuming that adding more guidance improved the system.

I would want those evaluations grounded in the mistakes and tasks that matter to the team. Can the agent choose the correct package for a component? Does it run the relevant validation? Can it find an existing implementation instead of creating another one? Those are more useful questions than whether the instruction file appears comprehensive.

Where the correction belongs

The practical value of these layers is that they give me a better way to respond when an agent gets something wrong.

Sometimes the necessary information was never available. Sometimes it was documented, but the agent failed to follow it. Sometimes the implementation passed a narrow check while breaking something outside that check’s scope. Sometimes the code was fine, but the work duplicated or conflicted with something already underway.

Those are different failures, and they call for different improvements. Writing a longer prompt is not a particularly good response to all of them.

More of my work now involves deciding where engineering knowledge should live so that it remains useful beyond the current conversation. That may mean documenting an architectural decision, creating a better skill, adding a deterministic check, expanding a CI lane, or making related work discoverable through the graph.

None of this guarantees that the next agent will make the right decision. It gives the agent better information to work from and more useful ways to recognize and recover from mistakes.

If I keep making the same correction, I want to understand what keeps forcing that knowledge back through me. The next session should be able to benefit from what we already learned.
